newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sees 8.5-10 pct inflation at end 1998-paper.
newsitem.headline: Poland sees 8.5-10 pct inflation at end 1998-paper.

text.p: Poland's finance ministry, preparing for next year's budget, assumes end-1998 year-on-year inflation of 8.5 to 10 percent, a gradual slowing of economic growth and lower real interest rates, the daily Rzeczpospolita said on Saturday.
The ministry's financial policy and analysis department' preliminary estimate expected a worsening of the current account balance of payments deficit, the paper added.
It said more ambitious targets for cutting inflation could be set, if central bank and government policies succeeded, but the ministry expected upward pressure on pay and food prices.

"Therefore the ministry prefers caution and assumes that in December next year prices will be 8.5-10 percent higher than in December 1997," it reported, adding that this depended on hitting December 1997 inflation targets of 11.1-13.8 percent.
The government target for 1997 is 13 percent year-on-year.
The paper said the ministry, in the preliminary estimates, expected real GDP growth of 5.1-5.6 percent this year, but the assumptions for next year put it at 4.2-4.9 percent.
The main growth impetus would come domestic demand, although the increase in demand would slow to 5.7-6.3 percent from 6.8-7.3 percent estimated for the current year.
The analysis projected a deficit on the current account of the balance of payments of 7.3 percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1998, contrasting with about one percent in 1996.

"While in 1997 the surplus on the capital account of about $7 billion still balances the current account deficit, the 1998 deficit on this account may reach $10.5 billion and the surplus on the capital account ($7.6 billion) will be incapable of balancing it," the paper quoted the department as saying.
This would be due to a deepening deficit in goods exchanges to 11.2 percent in 1998 from 9.5 percent this year.
The ministry expected export growth would increase to 13-15 percent in 1998 from this year's anticipated 12-13 percent and imports growth would fall to 16.5-18.5 from 24-26 percent.
On interest rates, it said that if the central bank's Lombard rate held at an average of around 23.3 to 25.3 percent this year, next year it could be around 17.3 to 21.3 percent.
It said the ministry expected banks to narrow the difference between interest rates on credits and deposits.
Average annual rates on 12-month credits would be 16.8- 20.8 percent against this year's 23.3-25.3 percent.
The average annual interest on 12-month deposits would fall to 13.6-17.6 percent from this year's 20.4 percent.

It said the estimate predicted the crawling peg devaluation of the zloty against a basket of currencies could slow to 0.8 percent per month from the current one percent and would drop to a monthly average of 0.55 percent next year.
Unemployment is expected to drop to 12.2 percent at the end of this year and to 11.5 percent at the end of 1998, it said.
Enterprise sector pay growth would slip to 14.5-15.7 percent from an expected 18.9-20.1 percent in 1997, while those paid from the budget would get 1998 rises of 15.8-17.1 percent.
The ministry said budget revenues this year could be 0.8 percent lower than expected due to smaller inflows from income and excise tax.
Privatisation revenues next year were projected at 4.45 billion zlotys, the same as this year, the paper said.
